title: Ten-Second Message Throttle
statement:
Build a log filter that stops the same message from flooding the console. Each message text may be printed at most once every 10 seconds: if a message was last printed at time t, it may print again at time t + 10 or later.

  • MessageThrottle() creates an empty filter.
  • shouldPrint(timestamp, message) returns true if the message may be printed now (and records that it was), or false if it must be dropped.

A dropped message does not restart its 10-second wait; only printed messages do. Timestamps are in whole seconds and never decrease from one call to the next. Several calls may share a timestamp.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the filter. The output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: "boot" printed at 1 is blocked until 11. At 11 it prints again. "disk" is a different message with its own clock.
The drop at 9 does not reset anything, so 10 is allowed. That print at 10 blocks 19.

hints: To decide about a message you only need one fact about its past. Which one?
Remember, per message, the time it was last printed. Not the last time it was seen.
A hash map from message to the last printed time. Allow the print if the message is new or the stored time is at least 10 seconds old, and only then update the map.

explain.intuition:
Each message has its own clock, and the only thing that clock needs is when the message last printed. A hash map from message text to that time answers every call in O(1): if the message is missing or the stored time is 10 or more seconds ago, print and store the new time; otherwise drop it and leave the map alone.

This is a throttle, the cousin of the debounce you write for scroll handlers: the first event goes through, then the gate stays shut for a fixed time. Leaving the stored time alone on a drop is what makes it a throttle rather than a debounce.
steps: Keep a map lastPrinted from message to timestamp.
If it is missing or t − lastPrinted[m] ≥ 10, set lastPrinted[m] = t and return true.
Otherwise return false without changing the map.
pitfalls: Updating the time on a dropped call too. That turns the throttle into a debounce, and in example 2 the call at 10 would be dropped.
Using > 10 instead of ≥ 10. Exactly 10 seconds later is allowed.
The map grows with every distinct message forever. Fine here, but a long-running service needs to evict entries older than 10 seconds (see the follow-ups).

complexity.time: O(1) per call (plus hashing the message)

solutions.title: Scan the print history
solutions.idea: Keep every printed (time, message) in a list and search backwards for a recent print of the same message.
solutions.time: O(p) per call, p prints so far

solutions.title: Map of last print times
solutions.idea: Store the last printed time per message; compare and update only on a print.

followups: Keep memory bounded to the messages printed in the last 10 seconds. What do you add next to the map?
Several servers share one throttle. Where does the state live, and what can go wrong between the check and the update?
